segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for November 4th, 2026.
Today we cover breakthroughs in learning robots, exciting mergers, and new humanoid developments.
Tune in for the full update.
From Humanoids Daily, LiberAI Unveils Liber-0: Learning from Human Experience for Zero-Shot Robot Manipulation.
This report details the introduction of Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on over two point two million hours of human experience to enable zero-shot robot manipulation.

The model integrates broad visual learning with glove-recorded motion and kinematic alignment to facilitate human-to-robot transfer, utilizing grounding human video in measured actions to learn behaviors not present in robot demonstrations.
Liber-0 successfully demonstrated zero-shot manipulation on tasks generated by GPT-6, achieving thirty-six point zero percent overall task success.
This development indicates that accumulated human experience can effectively guide robotic systems when coupled with reliable action grounding and embodiment alignment.
Future research will focus on scaling this transfer methodology across diverse manipulation tasks.
From Humanoids Daily, Churchill XI Shareholders Approve Agility Robotics Merger Ahead of Expected November 4 Closing.
This report details the successful shareholder approval for the merger between the SPAC Churchill Capital Corp XI and Agility Robotics, with the transaction anticipated to close around November 4.

The transaction involved approximately four hundred sixty-five million dollars in gross capital, incorporating existing funding and a private investment, and over eighty-four percent of votes cast supported the combination during the November two meeting.
This approval represents a significant step toward a public listing for Agility Robotics, with the combined entity expected to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT on November five.
This development signals further integration within the robotics sector as the combined entity moves toward a public market valuation.
From Humanoid.guide, Minerva unveils Roger 1.0 humanoid for ordnance disposal.
This report details the introduction of a new humanoid system designed for explosive ordnance disposal and hazardous materials response.
The Roger 1.0 system operates as a remotely supervised tool, allowing an operator to control it via a virtual reality headset and haptic gloves.
The robot incorporates Minerva Intelligence, an internal artificial intelligence that enables navigation and movement based on operator input.
The design prioritizes intuitive manipulation by mirroring the operator's body for enhanced control.
This robot is intended for managing CBRN threats and emergency response, with industrial trials scheduled for oil and gas projects this autumn.
The development signals further advancements in physically intuitive robotics and remote operation capabilities.
From Humanoid.guide, Figure 03 humanoids walk out of BotQ in new campus footage.
This report details video evidence of newly manufactured Figure 03 humanoids moving across a company campus.
The approximately nineteen-second video, posted by founder Brett Adcock, captures white and black robots traversing a pedestrian walkway near a parking lot.
BotQ has manufactured over one thousand humanoid robots in total, which is distinct from the units featured in the campus footage.
Prior endurance testing indicated that a Figure 03 successfully completed a nine-day treadmill test covering three hundred forty-eight miles.
The robots observed in the video are equipped with cameras, fingertip tactile sensors, and wireless charging capabilities.
This progression indicates ongoing development in humanoid robotics and advanced locomotion technology.
From MIT News - Robotics, "Dream, build, destroy, repeat".
This report details the experience of members of the MIT Combat Robotics Club who learn through the cycle of building, battling, destroying, and repeating.
The club competes in the National Havoc Robot League, designing and competing with robots such as ARES and CHONKIV.
The team processes losses as opportunities for improvement, cultivating a sense of pride irrespective of the results achieved.
New members engage in an onboarding process where they construct small combat robots in teams, receiving hands-on education in engineering skills through collaborative, self-taught projects.
This iterative approach emphasizes practical application in robotics engineering.
The sustained focus on iterative development provides a model for practical, outcome-based learning in technological innovation.
From The Robot Report, "New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors".
This report details the publication of a new international standard designed to facilitate communication among industrial mobile robots irrespective of the manufacturer.
The key finding is the establishment of common requirements for automated guided vehicles, autonomous mobile robots, and similar systems operating within the same facility.
The new standard specifies the methods by which mobile robots, fleet managers, and other equipment can exchange essential data including location, speed, and tasking information.
This interoperability is intended to enhance system efficiency by mitigating robot interference and increasing operational availability.
The standard further addresses communication protocols with external systems such as enterprise resource planning tools and building automation systems.
This development establishes a unified framework for multi-vendor robotic coordination.
The industry should monitor the adoption rate of this standard across industrial automation sectors.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Humanoid Robots in Warehouses vs AMRs: Which Automation Makes Sense in 2026?".

This story examines the comparative viability of Autonomous Mobile Robots and humanoid robots for warehouse automation, finding that AMRs are recommended as the initial investment due to faster deployment and clearer payback.
Autonomous Mobile Robots are proven effective for moving inventory, optimizing travel paths within the warehouse environment.
Humanoid robots present the potential for automating manipulation tasks within human-designed spaces, focusing on object handling, which necessitates more complex training data acquisition.
The successful implementation of either system depends on the specific task fit, operational costs, and the quality of data utilized for robot learning.
Operators are advised to utilize AMRs for travel optimization while piloting humanoid systems for specialized, complex manipulation requirements.
This trend indicates a necessary specialization in robotic deployment strategies across industrial automation sectors.
From Humanoids Daily, Tokio Marine HCC and Adrian Flux Launch UK Home Insurance for Humanoid Robots.
This report details the launch of the United Kingdom's first household insurance policy specifically designed for domestic humanoid robots.
The policy is offered through Adrian Flux's home insurance offering and is underwritten by Tokio Marine HCC International.
Coverage encompasses protection for the robot itself, damages it may cause, and personal liability, incorporating options for emergency recovery or safe disablement.
The coverage details include protection against damage, theft, and liability, with a specified limit of five thousand pounds for sudden damage to the home or belongings.
This initiative addresses the emerging insurance requirements associated with the ownership of domestic humanoid robots.
The development suggests a growing need for specialized insurance frameworks within the rapidly expanding field of artificial intelligence and robotics.
From Humanoids Daily, "RobotWorld 2026 Opens With Humanoids and Physical AI in Focus".
This report covers the RobotWorld 2026 event, which centered on humanoids and AI-driven manufacturing demonstrations.
The event took place from November 4 to 7 at KINTEX in Goyang, South Korea, and featured contributions from 402 companies representing seventeen nations.

The central themes of the conference focused on the integration of humanoids into production systems alongside existing equipment, with numerous demonstrations showcasing dexterous hands and advanced automation capabilities.

Exhibitors presented systems encompassing components, software, and complete machines designed for humanoid development, alongside dedicated tracks for manufacturing and physical artificial intelligence.
This focus signals an increasing industry concentration on tangible, embodied AI applications within industrial settings.
From The Guardian - Artificial Intelligence, "Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi".
This story examines the development and ethical implications surrounding the use of robot dogs in the pursuit of advanced artificial intelligence training data.
A startup named Dimensional employs individuals to walk robot dogs to collect the necessary training data for developing more autonomous AI operating systems.
This process highlights the growing intersection between robotics, data collection, and artificial intelligence development.

Furthermore, another entity, Warhound, is developing genetically modified dogs incorporating cybernetic augmentations and battlefield awareness, suggesting a potentially more aggressive trajectory for this technology.
The involvement of figures connected to weapons technology raises questions about the ultimate application of this research.
The piece explores the dystopian potential arising from the advancement of robotics and genetic modification in the context of artificial intelligence.
This development necessitates closer scrutiny of the ethical boundaries governing autonomous robotics and genetic engineering.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, RY H2!".
This segment reports on the introduction of the RY H2 robotic hand by Ruiyan Robotics and its initial assessment.
The robotic hand was introduced in March 2025 as an affordable option for the robotics market, achieving an overall score of four out of ten, placing it in the developing category.
Assessment scores for dexterity and strength further indicate a developing profile rather than a leading one for this device.

The product is currently listed as in production, offering an accessible entry point into the robotic hand market with a listed price of one thousand four hundred US dollars and a launch price of nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine Chinese Yuan.
The device demonstrates the manufacturing of an entry-level robotic hand.
This development suggests increased accessibility for robotic manipulation tools within the broader technology sector.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Y2-P!".
This segment reports on the introduction of a wheeled humanoid robot from Tlibot designed for adjustable sorting postures.
The platform features a torso capable of vertical lifting and forward pitching, enabling versatile manipulation.
The robot possesses a 700 millimeter torso lift and a working range of 2.19 meters, with each arm rated to carry a 5 kilogram payload.
The platform measures 156.5 centimeters in height and weighs 95 kilograms.
Obstacle avoidance is managed through integrated LiDAR, and the system is powered by an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, supporting software integration through ROS 2 and API.
The robot is commercially available at thirty-six thousand US dollars, focusing on providing a platform for research and goods sorting experiments.
This development indicates continued advancement in the application of mobile robotics for physical sorting tasks.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Dex2/5!".
This report details the specifications and status of the Dex2/5 robotic hand developed by Unitree Robotics for their G1 and R1 humanoids, noting its current production status.

The Dex2/5 is a lightweight robotic hand designed for integration into humanoid platforms, featuring a five-finger layout driven by two electric actuators, prioritizing mechanical simplicity over independent finger control.
The hand possesses a mass of three hundred sixty-five grams and is relatively compact for integration.
Performance assessments indicate that the hand is developing, with low scores noted for degrees of freedom and strength.
The unit is listed as in production with an advertised price of eight hundred dollars.
This development indicates ongoing work in achieving functional, lightweight manipulation tools for advanced humanoid robotics.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, TLIBOT T1!".
This report details the specifications and demonstrated capabilities of the TLIBOT T1, a humanoid research platform developed in Mianyang, China.

The robot is a 160 centimeter tall, 43 kilogram bipedal humanoid featuring forty-one body degrees of freedom and specific joint torque ratings including four hundred fifty Newton meters at the hip, two hundred eighty-one Newton meters at the knee, and one hundred forty-eight Newton meters at the ankle.
The platform incorporates a one thousand one hundred ten watt-hour battery allowing for a three-hour runtime and a maximum speed of three kilometers per hour.
Current demonstrated capabilities concentrate on obstacle avoidance and sorting goods, while navigation and manipulation scores remain low.
The platform is currently priced at forty thousand dollars and is designated for research and general-purpose humanoid applications.
This development indicates ongoing progress in creating functional, albeit specialized, robotic platforms for research purposes.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Y1!".
This report details the specifications and capabilities of the Y1, a wheeled humanoid robot from Tlibot.
The robot features a folding and lifting body for adjustable working height and dual arms capable of supporting five kilograms each.
The Y1 stands at one hundred ninety-five centimeters tall and weighs one hundred fifty kilograms, with a maximum travel speed of five point four kilometers per hour.
The system incorporates an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and utilizes LiDAR scanning for obstacle avoidance during navigation.
The dual arms are employed for sorting goods, achieving a combined sorting payload of ten kilograms.
The robot supports the ROS 2 framework for workflow development.
This development indicates advancements in mobile manipulation and autonomous navigation systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, MIDAS Hand!".
This report details the development of an open-source robotic hand designed for research into robot learning and manipulation.
The system, named MIDAS Hand, is an anthropomorphic sensing hand constructed from printed plastic and a soft TPU palm.
The project, developed by researchers at UCLA's RoMeLa laboratory, allows for the sharing of a design without reliance on commercial products.
Assessments of the system yielded a low overall score of four out of ten, reflecting that it is a developing system, with specific ratings provided for degrees of freedom and strength.
This open-source approach aims to increase accessibility to robotic hand research through shared designs and manageable hardware costs.
The findings indicate a step forward in democratizing the study of robotic manipulation techniques.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Fengxing-001!".

This segment details the specifications and demonstrated capabilities of the Fengxing prototype, an 180 centimeter tall, 80 kilogram humanoid developed by AVIC for aviation manufacturing and maintenance.

The prototype incorporates an electrohydraulic hybrid drive and compact leg motors derived from aero engine technology, exhibiting functions such as obstacle avoidance, jumping and landing, and product assembly.
Current skill ratings indicate ongoing development, with navigation and manipulation capabilities rated at a low level.
The robot remains a prototype with a listed price of one hundred fifty thousand US dollars, specifically targeting aviation industrial applications.
This development signals continued advancement in the integration of advanced robotics within the aerospace manufacturing sector.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, LUMO!".
This segment reports on the introduction of LUMO, a compact humanoid robot designed for companionship and various settings, with preliminary functionality in navigation and manipulation.
The robot measures one hundred thirty centimeters in height and is constructed with an aluminum alloy and plastic exterior.
LUMO is capable of performing basic obstacle avoidance and sorting tasks, operating at a maximum speed of five kilometers per hour, and utilizes electric bionic joints.

The device is listed at twelve thousand dollars and is intended for educational and research applications, demonstrating a low Humanoid Guide Skill Score indicating preliminary navigation and manipulation capabilities.
This development indicates ongoing progress in bridging companion design with basic physical task execution in robotics.
From The Robot Report, Ben Waters on the latest wireless charging strategies.
This report addresses the crucial role of charging strategy in optimizing robot fleet performance, affecting uptime, infrastructure, and battery size.
The strategy of opportunity charging, where robots autonomously move to charging stations when battery levels are low, is presented as an efficient wireless solution for managing large fleets.

Companies are advised to integrate power infrastructure planning and battery specifications into the initial system design process, viewing charging as an integral part of robot design rather than an afterthought.
Companies such as WiBotic are currently innovating by developing smaller, higher-power, and more robust wireless charging systems suitable for applications like drones and humanoids.
This development indicates a shift toward embedding energy management directly into robotic system architecture.
From Robohub, "Robots in society, business and culture: October 2026".
This segment examines developments in robotics across society, business, and culture, with key findings related to visual perception and technological advancements.
Researchers found that people perceive robots approaching from behind as moving faster than from the front, attributing this effect to visual turning behaviors.
Engineers developed biohybrid robots utilizing muscle tissue to achieve increased range of motion through electrical stimulation.
Furthermore, an artificial intelligence system was created for a racing drone to navigate complex courses using only a single camera.
The industrial robot startup RobCo reached a billion-dollar valuation and is planning the launch of a self-learning robot.
Various collaborations are currently advancing humanoid automation and artificial intelligence solutions across logistics, manufacturing, and artistic expression.
These developments signal continued integration of advanced robotics into practical applications across numerous sectors.
From Humanoids Daily, AiMOGA Opens Global Pre-Orders for MOBO Home Companion Robot.
This report details the launch of global pre-orders for MOBO, Chery's first home companion robot, signaling commercial interest in the product.
AiMOGA, Chery's robotics brand, opened global pre-orders for the MOBO home companion robot on October 21.
The device features twenty-two degrees of freedom and is engineered specifically for home companionship, incorporating capabilities for family-member recognition and long-term memory.
The robot operates using the MoAgent intelligent agent to manage spatial awareness, conversation, and motion control.
Chery positions robotics as an extension of its vehicle intelligence, with future integration being an objective.
Pre-orders have commenced, although specific pricing and delivery timelines have not been disclosed.
This development indicates growing market engagement for advanced domestic robotics integration.
And that's all the circuits for today's digest!
LiberAI's new zero-shot manipulation is truly a mind-bending move.
Thanks for powering up your knowledge with us.
Until tomorrow, keep building!
